title: Explicit expression and fast algorithms for the inverse of some matrices arising from implicit time integration

candidates.claim_content: Let c_0, c_1, ..., c_n be distinct numbers. For a fixed index i, let psi(x) = prod_{k=0, k≠i}^{n} (x - c_k), and write psi(x) = sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} sigma_{n-k}(c_0,...,c_{i-1},c_{i+1},...,c_n) x^k, where sigma_m denotes the elementary symmetric function of degree m of the n arguments c_0,...,c_{i-1},c_{i+1},...,c_n. The paper's Lemma 2.1 asserts that for i ≠ j, sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} k c_j^{k-1} sigma_{n-k}(c_0,...,c_{i-1},c_{i+1},...,c_n) = prod_{k=0, k≠j}^{n} (c_j - c_k). The left-hand side equals psi'(c_j) = sum_{m≠i} prod_{k≠i,m} (c_j - c_k), which for j ≠ i reduces to prod_{k≠i,j} (c_j - c_k), since all terms with m ≠ j contain the vanishing factor (c_j - c_j).
candidates.suspected_defect: The right-hand side in the i ≠ j case omits the exclusion of the index k = i: it should be prod_{k ≠ i, j} (c_j - c_k), not prod_{k ≠ j} (c_j - c_k). The two differ by the factor (c_j - c_i). The proof of the lemma, two lines later, correctly concludes prod_{k ≠ i, j} (c_j - c_k), so the lemma statement contradicts its own proof.

candidates.error_location: Equation (2.9), definition of the generalized binomial coefficient at i = 0
candidates.claim_content: The paper defines, for 0 < i < n, the generalized binomial coefficient of distinct numbers c_0,...,c_n by (2.8): binom(c_n, c_i) = [prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_n - c_k)] / { [prod_{k=0}^{i-1}(c_i - c_k)] [prod_{k=0}^{n-i-1}(c_{n-k} - c_i)] } = [prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_n - c_k)] / { (-1)^{n-i} prod_{k≠i}(c_i - c_k) }. It then extends the definition by (2.9): binom(c_n, c_n) = 1 and binom(c_n, c_0) = (-1)^n prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_n - c_k) / prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_{n-k} - c_0). The paper then asserts that setting c_i = i gives binom(c_n, c_i) = n!/(i!(n-i)!), and uses binom(c_n,c_0) in Theorem 2.2 / Corollary 2.3 / Theorem 2.4 (e.g. W_{0j} = (-1)^{j} binom(c_n,c_0) / (c_j - c_0) * binom(c_n,c_j)^{-1}).
candidates.suspected_defect: Setting i = 0 in the defining product (2.8) gives binom(c_n,c_0) = prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_n - c_k) / prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_{n-k} - c_0), with NO factor (-1)^n. The extra (-1)^n in (2.9) makes the definition inconsistent with (2.8) and with the stated binomial specialization: for c_i = i, (2.9) yields (-1)^n * n!/n! = (-1)^n, whereas binom(n,0) = 1. Consequently the second (binomial) form of W_{0j} in Theorem 2.2 and the formulas for (e_1^T V_n^{-1} C_n^{-1})_i and (-A^{-1} e)_i in Theorem 2.4 pick up a spurious sign (-1)^n. A direct check with n = 1, c_0 = 0, c_1 = 1 gives W_{01} = -1, while the binomial form with (2.9) would give +1.

candidates.exact_quote: (2.18) \quad V^T F = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & e_1^T \\ c_0 & V_n \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad H^T = F \begin{pmatrix} 0 & c_0^T \\ c_0 & C_n \end{pmatrix}.
candidates.claim_content: H is the (n+1)x(n+1) matrix (indices 0..n) whose only nonzero entries are H_{i,i-1} = i for i = 1,...,n (a strictly lower bidiagonal matrix with 1,2,...,n on the subdiagonal). F is the (n+1)x(n+1) shift matrix with F_{i,i+1} = 1 for i = 0,...,n-1 and zeros elsewhere. C_n = diag(c_1,...,c_n) and D_n = diag(1,2,...,n), and the vector c_0 = (c_0, c_0^2, ..., c_0^n)^T, which is the zero vector under the theorem's hypothesis c_0 = 0. The paper claims H^T = F * [[0, c_0^T],[c_0, C_n]].
candidates.suspected_defect: H^T has superdiagonal entries 1,2,...,n, i.e. H^T = F * diag(0,1,2,...,n) = F * [[0,0],[0,D_n]]. The paper writes C_n = diag(c_1,...,c_n) instead of D_n = diag(1,...,n); the identity as written is false unless c_i = i. Indeed the very next display (2.19) substitutes D_n in this position, so (2.18) contradicts (2.19).

candidates.error_location: Section 2 (text preceding Eq. (2.2)) and Lemma 2.1 preamble: definition of the elementary symmetric functions
candidates.exact_quote: where \(\sigma_{n+1-k}\) denotes the \(k\)th elementary symmetric function of \(c_0, c_1, \cdots, c_n\), i.e., \(\sigma_{n+1-k}(c_0,c_1, \cdots, c_n)\) is the sum of all distinct products of \(k\) of the arguments
candidates.claim_content: The paper defines sigma_{n+1-k}(c_0,...,c_n) to be 'the kth elementary symmetric function', i.e. the sum of all distinct products of k of the arguments c_0,...,c_n, and similarly in Lemma 2.1 defines sigma_{n-k} to be 'the kth elementary symmetric function of c_0,...,c_{i-1},c_{i+1},...,c_n'. With these conventions the paper then writes, via Vieta's formula, varphi(x) = prod_{k=0}^{n}(x - c_k) = sum_{k=0}^{n+1} (-1)^{n+1-k} sigma_{n+1-k}(c_0,...,c_n) x^k (Eq. 2.2) and psi(x) = prod_{k≠i}(x - c_k) = sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} sigma_{n-k}(c_0,...,c_{i-1},c_{i+1},...,c_n) x^k (Eq. 2.5).
candidates.suspected_defect: The verbal definition conflicts with the subscript used in the formulas. Vieta's formula requires the coefficient of x^k in prod_{j=0}^{n}(x-c_j) to be (-1)^{n+1-k} e_{n+1-k}, where e_m is the sum of products of m distinct arguments; i.e. sigma_{n+1-k} must be the sum of products of (n+1-k) arguments, not of k arguments as the text states. With the stated definition, (2.2) and (2.5) are false (e.g. for n = 1, c_0 = 0, c_1 = 1 the stated convention would give the wrong constant term).

candidates.exact_quote: A straightforward calculation shows that complexity for computing $\tilde{g}$ and $\tilde{W}$ are $2n^2$ and $n^2 + n$, respectively. Finally, we obtain Algorithm 3.3 with the complexity $7n^2 + 9n$ flops.
candidates.claim_content: Algorithm 3.3 consists of three steps: (i) compute the matrix G (with G_{ii}=1 and G_{ik}=c_i-c_k for i≠k, of size (n+1)x(n+1)), for which the paper states the cost is (n+1)^2 flops; (ii) compute the vector tilde{g} with tilde{g}_i = psi(c_{i+1})/psi(c_i), stated cost 2n^2 flops, and then the matrix tilde{W} with tilde{W}_{ij} = psi(c_j)/psi(c_i) by the recursion tilde{W}_{ij} = tilde{W}_{i(j-1)} tilde{g}_{j-1} and tilde{W}_{ij} = 1/tilde{W}_{ji}, stated cost n^2+n flops; (iii) compute W from tilde{W} and G by W_{ij} = tilde{W}_{ij}/(c_j-c_i) for i≠j and W_{ii} = sum_{k≠i} 1/G_{ik}, for which the paper states the cost is 3n^2+7n flops. The paper then concludes the total complexity of Algorithm 3.3 is 7n^2 + 9n flops.
candidates.suspected_defect: Adding the paper's own component counts gives (n+1)^2 + 2n^2 + (n^2+n) + (3n^2+7n) = 7n^2 + 10n + 1, which does not equal the stated total 7n^2 + 9n. The stated total is inconsistent with the stated parts.

candidates.exact_quote: From the above analysis, we observe that it requires \(7n^2 + 15n\) operations to compute \(W\).
candidates.claim_content: Algorithm 3.2 consists of: (i) computing G ((n+1)x(n+1) matrix with G_{ii}=1, G_{ik}=c_i-c_k), stated cost (n+1)^2 flops; (ii) computing the first row tilde{W}_{0j} = prod_{k=0}^{n} G_{jk}/G_{0k}, stated cost 2n^2+4n flops; (iii) forming g = (1/tilde{W}_{01}, ..., 1/tilde{W}_{0n})^T and then tilde{W}_{ij} = tilde{W}_{0j} g_i, stated cost n^2+n flops; (iv) computing W from tilde{W} and G, stated cost 3n^2+7n flops. The paper concludes the total is 7n^2+15n operations.
candidates.suspected_defect: Summing the paper's own stated component costs gives (n+1)^2 + (2n^2+4n) + (n^2+n) + (3n^2+7n) = 7n^2 + 14n + 1 (or 7n^2+15n+1 if the n reciprocals of (3.7) are counted), neither of which equals the stated 7n^2 + 15n. The announced total does not match the sum of the parts.

candidates.claim_content: Example 3 of the paper claims that the n+1 points c_i = 1/2 + (1/2) cos((2i+1)pi/(2n+1)), i = 0,1,...,n, are 'Chebyshev nodes in (0,1)', i.e. the n+1 Chebyshev points of the first kind mapped to the open interval (0,1).
candidates.suspected_defect: With the denominator 2n+1 and i running over 0,...,n, the last node is c_n = 1/2 + (1/2)cos((2n+1)pi/(2n+1)) = 1/2 + (1/2)cos(pi) = 0, which is not in the open interval (0,1). The n+1 Chebyshev points of the first kind on (0,1) require the denominator 2(n+1) = 2n+2, giving cos((2i+1)pi/(2n+2)). As written the set is not the Chebyshev point set and violates the stated interval.

candidates.error_location: Section 2.2 (definition of Radau IIA nodes) and Example 2
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that the collocation nodes c_i (1 <= i <= n) for the n-stage Gauss and Radau IIA implicit Runge-Kutta methods are the zeros of d^n/dx^n (x^n (x-1)^n) and of 'd^n/dx^{n-1} (x^{n-1}(x-1)^n)', respectively. The same expression is repeated in Example 2 of Section 4.
candidates.suspected_defect: The second differential operator is malformed: the order of differentiation in the numerator (n) does not match the denominator (dx^{n-1}). The Radau IIA nodes are the zeros of d^{n-1}/dx^{n-1} (x^{n-1}(x-1)^n), a polynomial of degree n. As written, d^n/dx^{n-1} is undefined / inconsistent, and if read as the n-th derivative of a degree-(2n-1) polynomial it would give a degree n-1 polynomial with only n-1 zeros, not n nodes.

candidates.error_location: Section 1 (Introduction) versus Section 2.2 (formula for the BIM inverse N)
candidates.exact_quote:
i.e., the inverse of IRK matrix and BIM matrix is exactly \( W_n^T \) if \( c_i \) (\( 1 \leq i \leq n \)) are
the zeros of the Legendre polynomials and \( c_i = i \) (\( 1 \leq i \leq n \)), respectively.
candidates.claim_content: The introduction claims that the inverse of the block implicit method (BIM) matrix is exactly W_n^T when c_i = i (1 <= i <= n), where W = V^{-1} H V with V the Vandermonde matrix on nodes c_0,...,c_n, H the matrix with subdiagonal entries 1,...,n, and W_n the trailing n x n block of W. Section 2.2, however, states that the inverse of the BIM matrix is N = D_n (V_n D_n V_n^{-1} D_n^{-1}) D_n^{-1} + D_n^{-1}, where D_n = diag(1,...,n), V_n is the n x n Vandermonde matrix on c_1,...,c_n with c_i = i, and (by (2.16) with C_n = D_n when c_i = i) V_n D_n V_n^{-1} D_n^{-1} = A^{-1} = W_n^T.
candidates.suspected_defect: The two statements are inconsistent: Section 2.2 gives N = D_n W_n^T D_n^{-1} + D_n^{-1}, i.e. a diagonal similarity transform of W_n^T plus a diagonal term, which is not equal to W_n^T in general (already for n = 2 the two differ). The introduction's claim that the BIM inverse 'is exactly W_n^T' therefore contradicts the paper's own Section 2.2.

candidates.exact_quote: In each step, both Algorithm 3.2 and Algorithm 3.3 can be implemented in parallel since the computations of each row of $G$, $\tilde{W}$ and $W$ are independent.
candidates.claim_content: The paper claims that in each of the three steps (computing G, computing tilde{W}, computing W) of Algorithms 3.2 and 3.3, the rows can be computed independently (hence in parallel). In Algorithm 3.2, tilde{W} is computed by first forming the whole first row tilde{W}_{0j} = prod_k G_{jk}/G_{0k} (0 <= j <= n), then setting g_i = 1/tilde{W}_{0i} and tilde{W}_{ij} = tilde{W}_{0j} g_i. In Algorithm 3.3, the strictly upper triangular part of tilde{W} is computed by the recursion tilde{W}_{ij} = tilde{W}_{i(j-1)} tilde{g}_{j-1} and the strictly lower triangular part by tilde{W}_{ij} = 1/tilde{W}_{ji}.
candidates.suspected_defect: The rows of tilde{W} are not independent in either algorithm: in Algorithm 3.2 every row i >= 1 requires the previously computed row 0 (tilde{W}_{0j} and g_i = 1/tilde{W}_{0i}); in Algorithm 3.3 the lower triangular entries of row i are obtained by (3.12) from entries tilde{W}_{ji} lying in other rows j < i. Hence the stated justification for row-wise parallelism in the second step is incorrect.
